source.title: A Systematic Empirical Study of Grokking: Depth, Architecture, Activation, and Regularization
source.authors: Shalima Binta Manir; Anamika Paul Rupa

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study trains small networks on modular arithmetic and measures training and test accuracy and grokking delay, directly reproducing the core training-and-evaluation setup. It also sweeps depth, architecture, activation, and weight decay.
record.gate_note: The study reports direct grokking outcomes, weight-decay outcomes, post-grokking Fourier measurements, and weight norms at grokking. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows. No training-set-size sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study trains MLPs and a 1-layer Transformer on modular addition and multiplication mod 97 with a 20% split. It measures training versus test accuracy and the step delay between them, which is the original grokking measure. It adds depth, architecture, activation and weight-decay sweeps, weight-norm tracking and a post-grokking Fourier analysis of embeddings.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that weight decay is the dominant control parameter, with a narrow Goldilocks range, and that grokking is governed by optimization stability interacting with regularization. Architecture has a real but moderate effect (1.90× at optimal λ). Activation effects depend on the regime. Grokking occurs at a consistent, width-dependent weight-norm threshold. All grokked models form sparse Fourier embeddings, with Transformers using different frequencies from MLPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study explicitly reproduces canonical grokking on modular addition and uses the training-accuracy/test-accuracy delay measure. It uses its own mod 97 task split, architectures, optimizer settings, and controlled sweeps rather than reproducing the original paper's complete experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with depth and stabilization (flat versus residual MLP), architecture-specific optimizer and weight decay, activation, and weight-decay strength. The paper reports an activation-by-regularization interaction and different grokking success rates across seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: The Transformer–MLP delay ratio depends on regularization choice: 1.11× at H2 configs, 1.90× at each architecture's optimal λ, and 1.42× on multiplication.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reported architecture differences in grokking delay are largely confounded by optimizer and weight-decay choices.

fits_no_version.finding: The weight norm at grokking is similar across activations (GELU 0.0225 vs ReLU 0.0219), while ReLU takes much longer to reach it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The activation function sets the rate of norm decay toward a width-dependent norm threshold, not the threshold itself.

record.problems: The study uses a fixed training fraction, so it does not test the smaller-training-set delay claim. Several configurations have only 3–5 seeds, and the weight-norm and Fourier analyses use one seed per configuration. DNF outcomes are bounded by finite training budgets. The paper states that architecture comparisons use different optimizers and regularization regimes, so architecture is not fully isolated.
record.rows_left_out: Seed-level outcomes and some individual settings were not separately extracted where the paper also reports aggregate outcomes. The full per-seed rows in Tables 2–4 and 9–10 are not all included; aggregate summaries and notable failures are retained. The complete weight-decay sweep conditions are included in r22–r34.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size. The split is fixed at 20%; the claim that larger fractions remove the delay is stated without data.
All of it: no tracking of circuit formation or memorization removal during training, and no progress measure tested for anticipating the jump. The Fourier analysis is post-grokking only.
All of it: no non-algorithmic data, no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich manipulation.
All of it: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Critical dataset size, ungrokking below it, and whether the low-norm solution is a more efficient circuit.
Convergence across seeds within an architecture, which uses seed 0 only. Identification of the algorithm beyond embedding spectra, e.g. logits or attention/MLP circuits.
Floating-point or softmax artifacts and adaptive-optimizer instabilities are not controlled or tested.

missing.what: Activation comparison on modular multiplication: GELU 5/5 at 24,400 ± 3,578; ReLU 5/5 at 93,200 ± 47,045; Tanh 3/5 at 102,667 ± 19,732.

Weight-norm trajectories: a gradual decay from ~0.1–0.4 to a plateau, with grokking near the bottom, plus per-config train/test curves. This is a continuous measure preceding the jump, not recorded as a time series.

record.verdict_notes: Several internal inconsistencies: ReLU delay is 180,000 in Table 7 but 80,000 in Table 8; the GELU/ReLU timing ratio is 6.9× in Exp 6 but 3.1× in Exp 7; Table 7's Transformer λ=5 delay is 12,000 vs a 24,000 mean in Table 6. Norm and Fourier analyses use one seed per configuration. MLPs grok with full-batch SGD with momentum, so the delay here does not need an adaptive optimizer. This bears loosely on the adaptive-optimizer part of V7, but no control or test of V7 is run, so no V7 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses a fixed 20%/80% split; it does not vary training-set size or test whether smaller training sets require more optimization.

Fourier representations are measured after grokking, but the study does not track gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or whether continuous progress measures anticipate the accuracy transition.
No non-algorithmic dataset, initialization-scale intervention, or lazy-to-rich transition test.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning.

Weight decay is swept and weight norms are measured, but the study does not test whether lower-norm solutions are more efficient circuits, nor the predicted critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
Fourier spectra are compared across three model configurations, using seed 0; the study does not establish whether runs within each architecture and configuration converge to the same algorithm.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts, or whether controlling them removes grokking.

rows.subject: 2-layer MLP (width 256, GELU), seed 0
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition mod 97; training and test accuracy tracked
rows.measure: Training accuracy reached 100% at Ttrain = 1,000; test accuracy was near chance (≈19.9%) for thousands of subsequent steps, crossed 99% at Tgrok = 33,000, and stabilized at ≈99.35%. ∆T = 32,000 steps.
rows.value: Ttrain = 1,000; Tgrok = 33,000; ∆T = 32,000 steps; test accuracy ≈99.35% after grokking
rows.note: Single reported seed.
rows.check: The paper calls the 19.9% test plateau near chance, but chance for 97 classes is about 1%. Ttrain is 1,000 in Fig. 1 text but 2,000 for depth-2 seed 0 in Table 2, and the training set is given as 1,882 vs ≈1,883 pairs.

source_check.correct: State: partial for V1. Delayed near-perfect generalization is reported, but the stated 19.9% plateau is above chance for 97 classes. Section 5.1 gives Ttrain=1,000 and Tgrok=33,000; Table 2 gives 2,000 and 34,000 for depth-2 seed 0. Both give delay 32,000.
source_check.problem: The reported numbers are present, but the stated test plateau does not support the chance-level component of V1.

relationships.condition: MLP (SGD) λ from 1e-5 to 1e-3 and Transformer (AdamW) λ from 0.01 to 5.0, plus weight norms at grokking
relationships.reason: With too little weight decay, models memorize but never grok (r22, r29). The MLP delay falls from 388k to 25k steps as λ rises (r23–r26). Grokking happens near the bottom of a norm decay, at ~0.022 across width-512 models (r35–r41).
